chapter: Life in New York in the 1940s
title: Lester Young and Coleman Hawkins: drinking and not eating
summary: Edison says whiskey killed Pres's and Hawkins's appetites and Dance connects liquor with a lack of sweets.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: And it's too bad. But Pres, he never was on anything.
Except in later years when he started to drink so much.

Yeah, he started drinking. And that was the beginning of his demise, you know, the whiskey. Because he never ate anything. He never had what you'd call a good appetite. And when he started drinking, naturally the alcohol will take your appetite. And he never did eat anything.
With Hawk, too, you know. He didn't eat, did he?
Couldn't eat, no. He couldn't eat. He wouldn't eat, not an egg.
He'd order sometimes and he'd seem as though he couldn't masticate.

Oh, yeah, he couldn't eat it. And Pres was the same way. He would order a good meal and take a bite of this and he would leave it. And, you know, his body was just saturated with alcohol. And Coleman was the same way in his later years.

Well, you know, you've explained something to me, really in that -- I don't know why it never occurred to me before but, you see, if you're a pot smoker and you have a taste for sweet things, then liquor doesn't go well with sweet things.
You know, real drinkers never eat any dessert.
That's for sure. That's for sure. Well, the alcohol is so --
They got their sugar from the alcohol.
Yeah, the sugar in the alcohol.
